name: Malgana
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Gargett, Andrew. 2011. A salvage grammar of Malgana, the language of Shark Bay, Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics 624.

new_statements.quote: Primary stress in Malgana is typically assigned to the initial syllable of words, regardless of the numbers of syllables of individual items. Secondary stress is assigned to syllables alternating to the right, away from the primary stressed syllable. [...] Variation from the above pattern is found in a number of words where long vowels in non-initial syllables apparently attract primary stress away from the initial syllable. [...] i. assign primary stress to the word-initial syllable, and ii. assign secondary stress to syllables alternating to the right of the initial syllable, unless iii. a long vowel occurs in a non-initial syllable (excluding the word-final syllable), in which case assign this syllable primary stress, and iv. if a long vowel occurs in a penultimate syllable, then assign antepenultimate syllable secondary stress
new_statements.citation: Gargett, Andrew. 2011. A salvage grammar of Malgana, the language of Shark Bay, Western Australia. Pacific Linguistics 624. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics, Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-624.
new_statements.locator: §2.4 Stress, pp. 19-20 (PDF pp. 32-33 of the ANU open-access file)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word whatever its length; secondary stress on every second syllable rightward (['na.ngi."ya.nu]). The one systematic deviation: a long vowel in a non-initial, non-final syllable pulls primary stress onto itself (["ga.'thaa."gu.du] 'Shark Bay', ["nga.'thaa.nu] 'drink-PST'), so the pattern is initial-default with a marginal weight (vowel-length) override; word-final syllables never take primary stress and are often reduced.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating rightward from the primary-stressed syllable; when a long-vowel penult takes primary stress the antepenult gets secondary stress; when a long-vowel antepenult takes primary stress the penult gets secondary stress (final syllable avoided). Trisyllables mostly show final secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels in non-initial syllables attract primary stress (gathaagudu, ngathaanu, yanaangu, with variants ngathanu/yanangu keeping initial stress when the vowel is short); ['wu.thuu.ga] 'spear' keeps initial stress despite a long second vowel (recorded once); ['wi.lyaa] 'seagull' keeps initial stress because a final syllable cannot be primary-stressed; thalaaba unassessable. Vowel length itself is only marginally contrastive (one minimal pair wilyaa/wilya) and may derive from loss of rr (Gathaagudu ~ Gatharrgudu).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; data are citation forms and elicited sentences from tape recordings of the last two speakers (Topsy Cross, Minnie O'Dene, Denham 1995, recorded by Doug Marmion); author flags all results as tentative given the tiny salvage corpus.
new_statements.identity_note: Gargett 2011 describes Malgana proper as spoken at Shark Bay / Denham (glottocode malg1242, ISO vml; also spelled Malkana, Maldjana, Madjana, Majanna). No dialect division is reported (Thieberger 1993 §4.3.8: 'Dialects: No information'). The Glottolog 1996 Thieberger reference is the web edition of the 1993 Pacific Linguistics C-124 handbook fetched sources here.

sources.note: §2.4 Stress, pp. 19-20: primary stress on the word-initial syllable regardless of word length, secondary stress on alternating syllables to the right; a long vowel in a non-initial, non-final syllable attracts primary stress (e.g. ["ga.'thaa."gu.du] 'Shark Bay'), with secondary stress then placed on the antepenult/penult so that a word-final syllable is never prominent; explicit four-step rule set given; based on 1995 recordings of the last two speakers.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page malg1242 (references: Austin 1988 for classification; Bowern 2011, Campbell et al. 2022 for endangerment) and Wikipedia 'Malgana language' (phonology inventory only, no stress; cites Gargett 2011 and an Irra Wangga illustrated wordlist).
sources.note: Neither says anything about stress; both point to Gargett 2011 as the only grammatical description.

sources.note: §4.3.8 Malkana, pp. 87-88, is a catalogue entry only (names, classification, 'Grammar or sketch grammar: None', wordlists Barlee 1886b, Brandenstein 1966c, O'Grady 1959). Nothing on phonology or stress.
